label: Titus 1:5
text:
"Left" translates apoleipō (ἀπολείπω), a verb for a temporary leaving-behind, not the permanent departure implied by its cousin kataleipō — Paul's stay in Crete with Titus was meant to end, with Titus staying on only to finish the job.

"Set in order" is epidiorthoō (ἐπιδιορθόω), a term doctors used for splinting a broken limb or straightening a crooked one; the churches in Crete weren't broken beyond repair, just still bent, needing the adjustments Paul hadn't gotten to.

Those remaining tasks are literally "the things left" (ta leiponta), unfinished business rather than failures.

"Ordain" is kathistēmi (καθίστημι), literally "set down" — to install someone into a standing office — and "appoint" near the end is diatassō (διατάσσω), "give a charge," the word for issuing a formal directive. Titus wasn't left with vague suggestions; he had marching orders.
translation: For this reason I left you behind temporarily in Crete, so that you might set straight the things still left undone, and might appoint elders in every city, as I directed you.

label: Titus 1:6–9
text:
"Blameless" is anegklētos (ἀνέγκλητος): egkaleō means to bring someone up on formal charges, and the alpha-prefix negates it — not sinless, but a life offering no legal opening for an accusation to stick.

"Riot" translates asōtia (ἀσωτία), built from the negative of sōzō, "to save" — it names a life that can't be salvaged, money and character both poured out past recovery.

"Unruly" is anupotaktos (ἀνυπότακτος), "un-subjectable," a child who won't come under anyone's control.

"Steward" is oikonomos (οἰκονόμος), from oikos ("house") and the root behind nomos ("law, management") — the overseer runs God's household the way a steward runs an estate, accountable for what isn't his own.

"Self-willed" is authadēs (αὐθάδης), literally "self-pleasing" (autos + hēdomai) — a man whose own satisfaction is his final court of appeal.

"Soon angry" is orgilos (ὀργίλος), the adjective form of orgē, "anger" — a short fuse built in, not just occasional flashes.

"Temperate" is egkratēs (ἐγκρατής), "having power over" — the same self-mastery Paul lists among the Spirit's fruit in Galatians 5.

"Holding fast" the trustworthy word is antechō (ἀντέχω), a grip strong enough to resist being pried loose.

The overseer must be able both to "exhort" (parakaleō, literally "call alongside," urging rather than commanding) and to "convince" or "convict" (elegchō), a word for cross-examining an opponent until he is forced to admit he is wrong.
translation: If anyone is beyond reproach, husband of one wife, with children who are believers, not open to the charge of reckless living or rebellion — for as God's household manager, the overseer must be beyond reproach — not self-pleasing, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for money, but hospitable, a lover of what is good, sound-minded, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the trustworthy word as it has been taught, so that he may be able both to encourage with sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.

label: Titus 1:10–11
text:
"Vain talkers" is mataiologos (ματαιολόγος), pairing mataios ("empty, resultless") with logos ("word") — talk that produces nothing, noise without substance.

"Deceivers" is phrenapatēs (φρεναπάτης), literally a "mind-deceiver" (phrēn, "mind," plus apataō, "deceive") — subtler than an outright liar, someone who plants a false impression in another person's thinking.

"To stop the mouth" is epistomizō (ἐπιστομίζω), built on stoma, "mouth" — the image is a bit forced into a horse's mouth to shut it.

"Subvert" is anatrepō (ἀνατρέπω), "to overturn, capsize" — these teachers aren't just misguiding individuals, they're flipping entire households (oikos) over.
translation: For there are many rebellious people, empty talkers and deceivers of the mind, especially those of the circumcision, whose mouths must be stopped — men who are overturning whole households, teaching things they should not, for the sake of dishonest gain.

label: Titus 1:12
text:
Paul quotes a Cretan poet turning his own countryman's words against the false teachers.

"Always" is aei (ἀεί), "perpetually, without exception" — the charge of lying is constitutional, not occasional.

"Slow bellies" literally reads gastēr argos (γαστὴρ ἀργός), "an idle stomach" — argos is built from a- privative plus ergon, "work," so "without work." The image isn't slowness of digestion but appetite that never does anything productive — men defined by their stomachs rather than their labor.
translation: A certain one of their own, a prophet of their own people, has said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies.

label: Titus 1:13–14
text:
"Sharply" is apotomōs (ἀποτόμως), from apotemnō, "to cut off" — the rebuke should be a clean, decisive cut, not a lingering scolding.

"Giving heed" is prosechō (προσέχω), literally "to hold toward" — more than listening, it's granting consent, letting something take hold of you.

The false teachers "turn themselves away" (anastrephō in the middle voice) from the truth — the verb puts the responsibility on them; nobody dragged them off, they turned themselves.
translation: This testimony is true. For this reason, rebuke them sharply, so that they may be healthy in the faith, not holding on to Jewish myths and commandments of men who are turning themselves away from the truth.

label: Titus 1:15–16
text:
The purity in view here is ceremonial, the kind bound up in man-made rules about clean and unclean, not moral purity — the same category Jesus addresses when he tells the Pharisees that unwashed hands don't defile a meal.

"Profess" is homologeō (ὁμολογέω), "to say the same thing" — an agreement in word.

"Reprobate" is adokimos (ἀδόκιμος): dokimos describes metal that has passed assay by fire; the alpha-prefix flips it to metal tested and rejected. These men claim to know God in word while failing the one test that matters, their own conduct.
translation: To the pure, all things are pure; but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure — rather, both their mind and their conscience have been defiled. They claim to know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being detestable and disobedient, and disqualified for any good work.

label: Titus 2:1
text:
"Thou" translates the emphatic pronoun su (σύ), set in sharp contrast to the false teachers just described — you, unlike them.

"Become" is prepō (πρέπω), "to stand out, be conspicuously fitting" — Titus's teaching should visibly match sound doctrine, the way a garment properly fits its wearer.
translation: But as for you — go on speaking the things that are fitting for sound teaching.

label: Titus 2:2
text:
"Aged men" is presbutēs (πρεσβύτης), a matter of years, not church office.

"Sober" is nēphalios (νηφάλιος), tied to nēphō, "to be free of wine, clear-headed."

"Grave" is semnos (σεμνός), "dignified, worthy of reverence."

"Temperate" is sōphrōn (σώφρων), built from sōs ("sound") and phrēn ("mind") — a mind kept healthy and in control of itself.

"Sound" in "sound in faith" is hugiainō (ὑγιαίνω), the ordinary Greek word for physical health, applied here to doctrine free of any diseased admixture.

"Patience" renders hupomonē, literally "remaining under" — not passive waiting but staying put under pressure without buckling.
translation: That aged men be clear-headed, dignified, sound-minded, healthy in the faith, in the love, in the patient endurance.

label: Titus 2:3–5
text:
"Behavior" is katastēma (κατάστημα), broader than conduct — it's bearing, demeanor, the whole way a person carries herself.

"Holiness" here is hieroprepēs (ἱεροπρεπής), built from hieron ("temple, sacred place") and prepō ("to be fitting") — behavior appropriate to something set apart for God, temple-grade reverence.

"False accusers" is diabolos (διάβολος) — the same word rendered "devil" elsewhere, a slanderer who hurls accusations across at someone.

"Given to much wine" uses the perfect participle of douloō, "to enslave" — the perfect tense marks a settled condition, not a bad habit but a completed enslavement.

"Teachers of good things" is one compound word, kalodidaskalos (καλοδιδάσκαλος), kalos ("good") fused to didaskalos ("teacher").

What follows, "they may teach" the young women, is actually sōphronizō (σωφρονίζω), a causative verb meaning "to bring someone to their senses, train them into soundness of mind" — coaching, not mere instruction.

"Keepers at home" is oikourgos (οἰκουργός), "one who works at the house" — active management, not confinement.

"Obedient" is hupotassō (ὑποτάσσω), a military term for ranking soldiers under a commanding officer — voluntary, ordered submission, not coercion.
translation: Older women likewise are to be reverent in bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teachers of what is good, so that they may train the young women to be fond of their husbands, fond of their children, sound-minded, pure, workers at home, kind, putting themselves in subjection to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be spoken against.

label: Titus 2:6–8
text:
"Sober minded" translates sōphroneō (σωφρονέω), the verb form of the same sound-mindedness word used of the older men and women — self-mastery is the one virtue Paul asks of every group in this chapter, worded a little differently each time.

"Exhort" remains parakaleō, urging rather than commanding — Titus is to call alongside, not bark orders.
translation: Urge the younger men likewise to keep themselves under control; in everything showing yourself a model of good works, in your teaching showing integrity and dignity, sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that the opponent may be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.

label: Titus 2:9–10
text:
"Be obedient" is again hupotassō, but here in the middle voice — the slave is to place himself under his master's authority, an act of the will rather than a status forced on him.

"Master" is despotēs (δεσπότης), our word "despot," absolute ownership and authority.

"Answering again" is antilegō (ἀντιλέγω), "to speak against" — more than a smart remark, it covers quietly working against the master's stated wishes.

"Purloining" is nosphizō (νοσφίζω), skimming off for oneself a portion of what was entrusted to one's care — embezzlement in miniature.

"Adorn" is kosmeō (κοσμέω), from kosmos, "an ordered, harmonious system" — good conduct doesn't just avoid embarrassing the gospel, it makes the teaching about God attractive, gives it order and beauty in the world's eyes.
translation: Urge slaves to put themselves in subjection to their own masters in everything, to give them satisfaction, not talking back, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that they may make the teaching of God our Savior attractive in every way.

label: Titus 2:11–15
text:
"Grace" is charis (χάρις): in ordinary Greek ethics it named a favor given freely, expecting nothing back, but always between friends. The gospel breaks that boundary — God's charis lands on people who were his enemies, not his friends, which is what makes it grace rather than reciprocity.

"Hath appeared" is epiphainō (ἐπιφαίνω), built on phainō, "to shine" — grace didn't arrive quietly, it broke into visibility.

"Teaching" is paideuō (παιδεύω), the root of "pedagogy" — training that includes correction and discipline, not just information handed over.

The grammar of "that blessed hope" and "the glorious appearing" matters: one article governs both phrases joined by "and," which in Greek means they describe a single reality, not two — "the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ" is one event, and one person is both God and Savior in that clause.

"For" in "gave himself for us" is huper (ὑπέρ), a preposition that can mean "instead of" as much as "on behalf of" — substitution, not just benefit.

"Redeem" is lutroō (λυτρόω), freedom purchased by paying a ransom price.

"Peculiar," finally, is periousios (περιούσιος), "over and above" the ordinary — not odd, but specially set aside, a people God claims as his own private possession beyond the general run of things.
translation: For the grace of God that brings salvation to all men has appeared, training us so that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live self-controlled and righteous and godly lives in the present age, continually looking for the blessed hope — the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ — who gave himself for us, in order that he might ransom us from all lawlessness and cleanse for himself a people set apart as his own possession, eager for good works. Keep speaking these things and exhorting and rebuking with full authority. Let no one look down on you.

label: Titus 3:1–3
text:
"Put in mind" is hupomimniskō (ὑπομιμνήσκω), a repeated, ongoing reminder, not a one-time announcement.

"No brawlers" is amachos (ἄμαχος), "not a fighter" (a- + machē, "battle").

"Gentle" is epieikeia (ἐπιείκεια), the quality of someone who has a right and doesn't press it to the limit — reasonableness that yields rather than insisting.

"Foolish" is anoētos (ἀνόητος), lacking understanding, and "disobedient" is apeithēs (ἀπειθής), literally "unpersuadable" (a- + peithō, "persuade") — not just rule-breaking but immune to reason.

"Living" is diagō (διάγω), "to lead [one's days] through" — the whole span of a life, not a single act.
translation: Keep reminding them to put themselves in subjection to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to be peaceable, reasonable, showing all gentleness to all men. For we too were once without understanding, unpersuadable, going astray, slaves to various desires and pleasures, spending our days in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another.

label: Titus 3:4–7
text:
"Love toward man" is philanthrōpia (φιλανθρωπία), phileō ("to love, be fond of") fused to anthrōpos ("man, mankind") — our word "philanthropy."

"Regeneration" is palingenesia (παλιγγενεσία), palin ("again") plus the verb "to become" — a becoming-again, a fresh start at the root rather than a patch-up.

"Washing" uses the noun from louō, which means a full bath, the whole body — distinct from the verb used of washing just the feet in John 13, which covers only a part. The regeneration Paul describes is total, not partial.

"Renewing" is anakainōsis (ἀνακαίνωσις), kainos ("new") plus ana ("again, up") — where regeneration marks the single moment of new birth, renewing describes the ongoing, repeated remaking that follows it, the difference between being born and growing up.
translation: But when the kindness and love for mankind of God our Savior appeared, he saved us — not by works done in righteousness that we ourselves performed, but according to his mercy — through the washing of new birth and the continual renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

label: Titus 3:8
text:
"Faithful" is pistos (πιστός), "trustworthy," describing the saying just given as reliable rather than merely believed.

"Affirm" carries an intensive prefix in the Greek, marking a steadfast, forceful assertion rather than a passing comment.

"Be careful" is phrontizō (φροντίζω), "to give careful thought to," and "maintain" is proistēmi (προΐστημι), literally "to stand before" — to take the lead in something, be out front doing it, not just approve of it from a distance. Believers are to be out in front of good works, not trailing behind them.
translation: Trustworthy is the saying, and concerning these things I want you to speak with steadfast confidence, so that those who have believed God may give careful thought to taking the lead in good works.

label: Titus 3:9
text:
"Avoid" is periistēmi (περιΐστημι) in the middle voice, "to turn oneself around" to get away from something — deliberate, active avoidance, not passive disinterest.

"Foolish" is mōros (μωρός), the root of our word "moron."

"Vain" is mataios (μάταιος), "empty, without result" — arguments that go nowhere and produce nothing.
translation: But turn yourself away from stupid controversies and genealogies and quarrels and fights about the law, for they are unprofitable and empty.

label: Titus 3:10–11
text:
"Heretick" is hairetikos (αἱρετικός), from haireō, "to take for oneself, choose" — originally naming someone who picks his own doctrine rather than receives what's handed down, a self-appointed authority, a factionalist.

"Subverted" is ektrepō (ἐκτρέπω), a medical term for a limb wrenched out of its joint — not just off the path but twisted out of true.

"Condemned of himself" is autokatakritos (αὐτοκατάκριτος), auto ("self") plus the verb "to judge down" — his own conduct hands down the verdict against him; no outside witness is needed.
translation: Reject a factious person after one or two warnings, knowing that such a one has been twisted out of joint and goes on sinning, standing self-condemned.

label: Titus 3:12
text:
"Be diligent" is spoudazō (σπουδάζω), "make every effort, hurry up and do it."

"Determined" renders krinō in the perfect tense — a decision reached in the past that still stands, settled and not being reconsidered. Paul isn't musing about where to winter; he's already decided and the decision holds.
translation: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have determined to spend the winter there.

label: Titus 3:13
text: "Lawyer" translates nomikos (νομικός), which in the New Testament regularly means an expert in the Mosaic law, not a member of a Roman legal profession — Zenas's expertise was in Scripture, not statute.
translation: Diligently send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that nothing may be lacking to them.

label: Titus 3:14
text: "Maintain" is again proistēmi, "take the lead in" — the same word used in verse 8, applied now to meeting real, pressing needs rather than staying unproductive.
translation: And let our own people also learn to take the lead in good works for cases of urgent need, so that they may not be unfruitful.

label: Titus 3:15
text: "Salute" is aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι), a warm greeting, a wish of well-being extended to someone, closing the letter on a personal note.
translation: All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
